profile.reading:
Per CyrusOne's own site (confirming Norwalk, CT as this facility's location) and two independent aggregator listings agreeing on 6 Norden Place as the street address (resolving a minor city-label discrepancy where one aggregator mislabeled the city as Stamford), this NYM5 building publishes 168,000 sq ft and 4 MW of IT capacity.

Wikipedia's CyrusOne entry states the company acquired Cervalis, a Connecticut-area data center and colocation provider, in July 2015 for approximately $400 million, the likely origin of CyrusOne's presence in this Connecticut/Hudson Valley New York cluster; CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten and was taken private in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) acquired the company for approximately $15 billion.

Since going private under KKR and GIP ownership in 2022, CyrusOne has continued expanding its US and international footprint; the company's own press materials cite roughly $1 billion in cumulative capital investment in its San Antonio, Texas campuses alone as of a January 2025 groundbreaking, indicating continued growth investment across its portfolio under private ownership rather than a broad slowdown following the take-private transaction.

In November 2021, KKR and GIP first announced the agreement to acquire CyrusOne in an approximately $15 billion transaction, one of the largest data center M&A deals of that period, reflecting broader private-equity and infrastructure-fund interest in colocation real estate that has also driven acquisitions of peers like QTS (by Blackstone) and CoreSite (by American Tower) around the same era; CyrusOne's current published portfolio language describes more than 50 mission-critical facilities worldwide, though the company's own site and Wikipedia give somewhat different approximate totals (over 40 versus more than 50), neither of which this registry treats as a precise, independently verified figure.

reading.body:
CyrusOne Norwalk is Connecticut's largest published data center with 4 MW of critical IT load capacity. At a typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, this translates roughly to 100 racks. The facility occupies 168,000 square feet at 6 Norden Place in Norwalk, placing it in the dense Northeast corridor where power constraints are acute.

This campus represents half of Connecticut's total published data center capacity of 8 MW across two facilities. The state has five mapped data centers on record, but most publish no specifications, meaning the true scope of Connecticut's installed base and its grid exposure remain unmeasured. Norwalk's published 4 MW is the largest single figure the state's operators have disclosed.

The facility's capacity is modest relative to leading AI infrastructure campuses elsewhere, which measure in hundreds of megawatts. Connecticut's grid already carries the burden of dense urban and industrial load. A 4 MW facility in this context claims power density that is significant at the state scale, even though it represents a fraction of what large-scale AI training now requires, and the building's actual current utilization and tenant mix are not published.
